Content:
In general, if [MATH: X \sim U[a,b]] is uniformly distributed, then [MATH: X] has the following probability density function:

Content:
[MATH: {(1)/(b − a),|a ≤ x ≤ b; 0,|otherwise]

Content:
We can use a continuous uniform distribution to model situations where all possible outcomes on a finite interval are equally likely.

Content:
For instance, suppose a dental receptionist wants to model the waiting time of a randomly selected patient. After observing a number of patients over several days, the receptionist notices that the waiting time is uniformly distributed between [MATH: 6] and [MATH: 14] minutes, inclusive.

Content:
Then, by letting [MATH: X] be the amount of time a randomly selected patient spends waiting, we can model the waiting time using the continuous uniform distribution:

Content:
[MATH: X \sim U[6,14]]

Content:
Therefore, [MATH: X] has the following probability density function:

Content:
[MATH: {(1)/(8),|6 ≤ x ≤ 14; 0,|otherwise]

Content:
With this model, we can now make predictions about patient waiting times.

Content:
For example, the probability that a randomly selected patient waits longer than [MATH: 9] minutes is equal to
[MATH: P(X ≥ 9)|= ∫_{9}^{14}(1)/(8)dx; = (1)/(8)∫_{9}^{14}dx; = (1)/(8)[x]_{9}^{14}; = (1)/(8)[14 − 9]; = (5)/(8).]

Content:
We can also calculate the mean waiting time by finding the expected value of [MATH: X\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: E[X]|= (a + b)/(2); = (6 + 14)/(2); = 10]

Content:
Therefore, the mean waiting time is [MATH: 10] minutes.

sections.normalized_html: The duration of a radio program is uniformly distributed between [MATH: 27] and [MATH: 34] minutes, inclusive. What is the probability that a randomly chosen program lasts less than [MATH: 30] minutes?
sections.readable_text: The duration of a radio program is uniformly distributed between [MATH: 27] and [MATH: 34] minutes, inclusive. What is the probability that a randomly chosen program lasts less than [MATH: 30] minutes?

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Let [MATH: X] represent the duration of the radio program. From the problem statement, we know that [MATH: X \sim U[27,34],] and we wish to compute [MATH: P(X < 30).]

In general, if [MATH: X \sim U[a,b],] then [MATH: X] has the following probability density function:

[MATH: {(1)/(b − a),|a ≤ x ≤ b; 0,|otherwise]

So, for our random variable [MATH: X \sim U[27,34],] we have the following probability density function:

[MATH: {(1)/(7),|27 ≤ x ≤ 34; 0,|otherwise]

Therefore,

[MATH: P(X < 30)|= ∫_{27}^{30}f(x)dx; = ∫_{27}^{30}(1)/(7)dx; = (x)/(7)|_{27}^{30}; = (30)/(7) − (27)/(7); = (3)/(7).]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
In general, if [MATH: X \sim U[a,b]] is uniformly distributed, then [MATH: X] has the following probability density function:

We can use a continuous uniform distribution to model situations where all possible outcomes on a finite interval are equally likely.

Content:
For instance, suppose a dental receptionist wants to model the waiting time of a randomly selected patient. After observing a number of patients over several days, the receptionist notices that the waiting time is uniformly distributed between [MATH: 6] and [MATH: 14] minutes, inclusive.

Then, by letting [MATH: X] be the amount of time a randomly selected patient spends waiting, we can model the waiting time using the continuous uniform distribution:

Content:
[MATH: X \sim U[6,14]]

Content:
Therefore, [MATH: X] has the following probability density function:

Content:
[MATH: {(1)/(8),|6 ≤ x ≤ 14; 0,|otherwise]

Content:
With this model, we can now make predictions about patient waiting times.

Content:
For example, the probability that a randomly selected patient waits longer than [MATH: 9] minutes is equal to
[MATH: P(X ≥ 9)|= ∫_{9}^{14}(1)/(8)dx; = (1)/(8)∫_{9}^{14}dx; = (1)/(8)[x]_{9}^{14}; = (1)/(8)[14 − 9]; = (5)/(8).]

We can also calculate the mean waiting time by finding the expected value of [MATH: X\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: E[X]|= (a + b)/(2); = (6 + 14)/(2); = 10]

Therefore, the mean waiting time is [MATH: 10] minutes.
